ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 4 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Voltaire

code.originalText: Review of resection pathology, diagnosis, geriatric assessment, trial without catheter, and shared decision on treatment

text.paragraph: Review of the resection pathology and a trial without catheter; decision on treatment. [S]

Voltaire returns a week after the transurethral resection and two days after the sick visit for a catheter-associated infection. He has been afebrile since yesterday morning on cefpodoxime, and the culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to it. The urine is pale pink without clots. Since the resection he has had a burning ache above the pubic bone and bladder spasms, worst in the evening, rated 5 of 10; acetaminophen when he remembers takes the edge off. He asked for something strong, saying that a friend has offered him drops made with opium. He has had no constipation on polyethylene glycol. The trial without catheter began this morning: the catheter was removed at 8 am and he voided 260 mL before this visit. He came with his assistant and wants to hear the results plainly and to decide today. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 2026-04-22; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Thin, alert, and engaged; temperature 36.9 C
Blood pressure 124/68 mmHg; heart rate 82, regular
Mild suprapubic tenderness; bladder not palpable after voiding; no masses
Visible blood in the urine for three weeks with clots, and a weak stream, straining, and frequent small voids, in a man of 83; under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem echoing his documented urinary complaints and last illness; superseded by the diagnosis at the third chronic-care visit.
Chronic urinary retention with overflow (post-void residual 460 mL at intake), worsened by a nightly anticholinergic sleep aid; drained by an indwelling catheter
S — Synthetic finding echoing the strangury and catheterization documented in his last weeks.
Acute kidney injury from bladder outlet obstruction (creatinine 1.68 mg/dL, from 1.1 mg/dL a year earlier)
S — Synthetic finding; it echoes, without asserting, the later encyclopedia term uremia.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms: prostate about 78 mL on CT, enlarged, firm, and smooth on examination, PSA 6.4 ng/mL with a PSA density of 0.08; no prostate biopsy, by shared decision
S — Synthetic diagnosis echoing the very large prostate described at the 1778 autopsy; whether that prostate was malignant is unknown (CLM-0012).

Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, keratinizing, posterior wall extending to the dome, muscle-invasive with extravesical extension (clinical stage cT3b N0 M0, stage IIIA), pure squamous histology without a urothelial component; treated with palliative-intent hypofractionated radiotherapy by shared decision

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis confirmed by resection pathology. His bladder disease at autopsy is documented (D); calling it squamous cell carcinoma is a 2025 retrospective interpretation (R, disputed).
Chronic constipation, lifelong by his account, with long use of laxatives and self-given enemas
S — Synthetic modern problem echoing his documented colic, purges, and enemas; no diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease is made.
Febrile catheter-associated urinary tract infection with Escherichia coli, five days after bladder tumor resection; treated with cefpodoxime and a catheter change; resolved
S — Synthetic intercurrent infection; it echoes, without asserting, the infected urine described in his last weeks (CLM-0009).

list.item:
Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, muscle-invasive (C67.4). Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the posterior wall and dome, invading muscle, with lymphovascular invasion and a mobile palpable mass under anesthesia; with the CT urography and clear chest CT, clinical stage cT3b N0 M0 (stage IIIA). Pure squamous cell carcinoma is uncommon outside regions where schistosomiasis is common; it responds less well to chemotherapy than urothelial carcinoma, and radical cystectomy offers the best chance of cure. The G8 screen is 11 of 17 (abnormal), with low weight, reduced mobility, and help needed for shopping and travel, though he is independent in self-care and thinking clearly; his creatinine is 1.22 mg/dL (eGFR 59). We discussed four paths in plain terms: radical cystectomy with an ileal conduit, with a substantial risk of complications and a long recovery at his age; daily radiotherapy over four weeks with bladder preservation; weekly palliative radiotherapy (36 Gy in six fractions) aimed at controlling bleeding and local symptoms with few visits; and symptom care alone. His goals are to stay at home, finish his play, and avoid long hospital stays, and he accepts that weekly radiotherapy is unlikely to cure the cancer. [S]
He chose weekly hypofractionated radiotherapy, 36 Gy in six fractions; the radiation oncology team will plan it next week.
The palliative care team will join his care now, alongside treatment.
Dr. Bergström-Nwosu agrees with the plan and will see him if bleeding, clots, or retention return.

Visible blood in the urine with difficult urination (R31.0). Explained by the bladder cancer, with an enlarged prostate and chronic retention; superseded by those diagnoses. [S]
Managed under the bladder cancer, retention, and prostate problems.

Chronic urinary retention (R33.8). Trial without catheter passed: voided 260 mL with a post-void residual of 140 mL on tamsulosin. IPSS 14. [S]
Continue tamsulosin.
Bladder scan at the next visit; teach him to watch for a falling stream, overflow, or pain.

Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (T83.511A). Improving on day 3 of cefpodoxime; organism sensitive; white count 8.2. [S]
Complete seven days.

Chronic constipation (K59.09). Regular now; an opioid would worsen it. [S]
Add senna two tablets at night with any oxycodone; continue polyethylene glycol.

Pain from the bladder cancer and resection. Suprapubic burning and spasm, 5 of 10, interfering with his evening work. Acetaminophen has been taken irregularly. He has no history of a substance use disorder or overdose, but he has long dosed himself with remedies of his own choosing, and he asked about opium drops offered by a friend, of unknown strength. The state prescription monitoring program shows no controlled prescriptions. A small supply of a short-acting opioid at the lowest dose, with naloxone and clear limits, is safer than unmeasured drops from others. [S]
Acetaminophen 1 g three times a day on a schedule (3 g a day at most).
Oxycodone 2.5 mg (half a 5 mg tablet) only if pain is not relieved, no more than three doses a day; 15 tablets, no early refills, one prescriber.
Naloxone nasal spray in the house, with his assistant shown how to use it.
No alcohol on days he takes oxycodone, no sleeping pills, and no drops or remedies from anyone else; doses kept in a locked box.
Review in two weeks.
